Indentation is already tracked in:
* https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/86092

So this should focus on the number formatting

Hello, I think I'll try my hand at this one, if everyone's alright with that. I have an assignment at school where I have to contribute to a large open-source project. I will focus on number formatting, as suggested. Could I be assigned, please?

> With Godot 4.4 not only the indents get changed, but also all number values get a ".0" if they were integer.

> I will focus on number formatting, as suggested.

In my opinion this doesn't need fixing. The JSON spec does not distinguish between `int` and `float`, so both `1` and `1.0` are correct. But the trailing `.0` makes things more obvious. We deliberately included this change in 4.4, see #47502 for details.

When saving JSON in 4.4 the stringification result changed, this is expected. I think the only debate here is whether the editor should automatically save and therefore reformat all `*.json` files, even if the user has not re-saved them. Note that if you change a JSON resource in the inspector and save it, it will be reformatted anyway.

> Could I be assigned, please?

You can start work without being assigned, we rarely use this GitHub feature. Sometimes priority issues are assigned to maintainers and active contributors, but it would be hard for us to track the progress on thousands of issues from hundreds of volunteer contributors.

If you have trouble choosing an issue, you can look at the [good first issue](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20state%3Aopen%20label%3A%22good%20first%20issue%22) label, an [issue triage project](https://github.com/orgs/godotengine/projects?query=is%3Aopen+Issue+Triage) for the area of ​​the engine you are interested in, or ask in the [contributors chat](https://chat.godotengine.org/). Good luck!

> I think the only debate here is whether the editor should automatically save and therefore reformat all *.json files

Could this be a user-selected setting maybe? Perhaps under Project Settings -> General -> FileSystem -> Import ?
I am all for an option to disable JSON resaving AND for an option to disable reformatting. My question still would be, why reformatting at all? What's the benefit?

I find it surprising that Godot has to overwrite the JSON for any reason in the first place. This will cause plenty of file locking issues on Windows. Due to this, Godot should *not* be rewriting *source* files. If it has to perform any rewriting, it should be strictly contained to `.godot/`. This is why the import system exists 🙂 

I guess what's happening here is that `json` is part of the TextFile extensions, so if you open the JSON in the script editor and run the scene, the usual indentation or trailing whitespace changes configured in the Editor Settings will apply. That part is intended. If you don't want this to happen, disable **Save Before Running** in the Editor Settings.

Is there a way to handle the issue where my ID fields, which are currently of type int/long, are being converted to float and causing all HTTP calls to the server using that ID to fail? For example, my server response looks like: {"id": 1234}, but when it's passed through Godot, it becomes 'id' = 1234.0, and if I send this ID back to the server, it results in a conversion error.
@duongxinh2003 That's a separate issue and that's because JSON doesn't work the way you think it does. It doesn't have integers

I couldn't reproduce the number reformatting in 4.4.1 or 4.5.dev3.
Are there more specific reproduction steps?
When I save a JSON file in the script editor, spaces change to tabs but all numbers stay the same.

Workaround: If you're not planning to edit the files _in the Godot editor_, then a "simple" workaround is to never `preload` the JSON file. If you manage it with just `load`s, Godot won't see fit to cannibalize your files.

---

But Godot should **absolutely** not be reformatting these files. The tabs vs spaces thing is an eternal debate and serves as a source of annoyance, but the numbers issue is an actual semantic bug.

> In my opinion this doesn't need fixing. The JSON spec does not distinguish between int and float, so both 1 and 1.0 are correct. But the trailing .0 makes things more obvious. We deliberately included this change in 4.4, see https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/47502 for details.

This is **incorrect**. The JSON spec defines a number as a sequence of numerical characters, and it chooses to remain agnostic about the representation. 1 and 1.0 are permitted to be distinct numbers according to the JSON spec, and it's up to the parser and implementing language whether they wish to treat those two as different. By blindly replacing 1 with 1.0, Godot is forcing its assumptions onto your JSON files and forcing any other tools that read those files to conform to Godot's assumptions as well.

Python's `json` library parses 1 as an int and 1.0 as a float, for instance. It's allowed to do that according to the JSON spec (which intentionally declines to have an opinion on the matter).
Will this be addressed in a future version of Godot? I find it really annoying that my commits are unnecessary big sometimes just because Godot decides to ad .0 to all the numbers.

This has been frustrating to deal with, my game leverages the Steam market and I keep the game's `itemdefs.json` file within the source code for the project. Godot will edit my item definitions adding unnecessary `.0`'s changing my integers to floats breaking the schema for Steam inventory service. My limited time Holiday items have a drop interval of `525600` minutes equaling 365 days or 1 year. Since Godot modified this to `525600.0` Steam ignored the property and set it to the my default configured economy server drop interval of `1440` or one day. This inadvertently devauled our limited time drop and players caught onto it before we realized. They farmed the limited drops hoarding or quick selling what was supposed to be a rare drop. We fixed it manually and increased the drop rate overall to compensate but are currently forced to store our item definitions outside of the game's source control.

If you don't want Godot to import your JSON files and treat them as resources it owns, you can change their import setting to "Keep (No Import)" in the Import tab (or configure it for all JSON files in the Project Settings' Import settings).

> If you don't want Godot to import your JSON files and treat them as resources it owns, you can change their import setting to "Keep (No Import)" in the Import tab (or configure it for all JSON files in the Project Settings' Import settings).

Is this AI generated? There are no import settings for JSON files.

No I'm not an AI... 😓 Just a spongy human meatbrain that can have memory shortcomings.
I thought JSON were made imported resources and would thus have import settings, but indeed after checking now this doesn't seem to be the case.

The only workaround I know of is to use a `.gdignore` file in the directory containing the JSON files. However, this has several drawbacks: 1. the directory won't appear in the File System dock, and 2. you won't be able to properly store resources in such a directory.

In my opinion, the main problem in this situation is that we're unsure whether we want to treat JSON as a full-fledged resource or as a simple text file. In 3.x, `JSON` was a singleton, not a resource. In 4.x, `JSON` became a resource editable via the editor UI. However, saving occurs from the parsed data, which loses formatting details that aren't relevant at the parsing stage.

Also, as far as I understand from the discussion, saving `JSON` resources is triggered automatically under certain circumstances, and not only when manually saving a `JSON` resource via the editor UI or via code (`ResourceSaver`). And this is the worst thing (above, I only advocated adding `.0`; this in itself is fine if you serialize data or save JSON as a `JSON` resource, not as a text file).

Possible solutions to this problem:

1. (Hard breaks compatibility) Turn JSON into a singleton or `RefCounted` class, in the spirit of 3.x. Treat JSON as a text file, not a resource.
2. (Soft breaks compatibility) Keep JSON as a resource, but make it read-only. Users will no longer be able to edit the resource through the editor UI. Saving via `ResourceSaver` will likely also be broken (we can leave it and restrict it to just the Inspector).
3. (Clutters the file system, does not completely solve the problem) Turn JSON into an imported resource with the `.import` file. Allows you to select the "do not import" option on a per-file basis.
4. (Doesn't completely solve the problem) Leave JSON as a resource, but ensure that saving the resource can only be triggered manually through the editor UI or through code (`ResourceSaver`), and cannot be triggered automatically when scanning the project with the editor, etc.
5. (Complex, redundant for parsing, can slow down parsing) Complicate the JSON parser so that it stores non-essential formatting details. When editing/saving a resource programmatically, formatting can only be changed for the affected elements, not for the entire parse tree.

> If you don't want Godot to import your JSON files and treat them as resources it owns, you can change their import setting to "Keep (No Import)" in the Import tab (or configure it for all JSON files in the Project Settings' Import settings). I don't see that option or project setting to change when selecting a .json file

> Why is JSON fundamentally different than a text file? @Mercerenies I explained above. Godot 4.x has a [`JSON`](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_json.html) resource type, and the [`ResourceFormatLoaderJSON`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/5b4cbd2299e867ec7d3b11fb2715e525e0f9fb8f/core/io/json.h#L109) and [`ResourceFormatSaverJSON`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/5b4cbd2299e867ec7d3b11fb2715e525e0f9fb8f/core/io/json.h#L123) classes are [registered](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/5b4cbd2299e867ec7d3b11fb2715e525e0f9fb8f/core/register_core_types.cpp#L245-L251) for the `json` file extension (so another workaround is to use a custom extension instead of `json`, like `mygamedata`). You can create and edit `JSON` resources through the Inspector UI: 1. If necessary, the Godot editor loads the `JSON` resource into memory: it parses the text file into an internal structure. 2. You can then make changes to this structure via the Inspector UI or the [`data`](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_json.html#class-json-property-data) property. 3. Finally, at some point, you click the Save Resource button or call the `ResourceSaver.save()` method. At this point, Godot generates a new text representation based on the internal structure. As I noted above, this structure doesn't store redundant data about the original JSON formatting, so this data is lost when saving. The biggest problem mentioned in this issue is that, under certain circumstances, step 3 can occur even without user interaction.

@dalexeev Thank you! I honestly never noticed there was an Inspector panel for JSON files. I see the point of contention now.

I think Option 3 is probably the best for everyone. It doesn't break existing workflows, but for those of us (like myself) whose workflows are **currently** broken, we can go into Project Settings and change the import settings to do the reasonable thing. I don't mind a bit more filesystem clutter. After all, we only just recently created `.uid` files for **every** asset, so what's a few more `.import`s?

> I think Option 3 is probably the best for everyone.

Personally, I'm leaning toward Option 4. In the long term (Godot 5), I'd suggest Option 1.

Option 2 also makes some sense for 4.x if the JSON file editing feature isn't very popular, but we should be careful about saving JSON resources (via `ResourceSaver`). And it probably doesn't make sense to only disable editing via the Inspector while still allowing saving via `ResourceSaver`.

Option 3 has the disadvantage not only of cluttering the filesystem with `.import` files, but also of introducing differences between format loaders and importers. We also specifically [disabled](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/99540) the generation of `.uid` files for `.json` because we want to treat them as text files rather than resources.

my 5c:
TBH, this is somewhat (but not fully) similar to the problems with CSV files. I wanted to use CSV for data storage in my game. Simply dropping a CSV into the editor treats the CSV as a translation resource and emits some files. I then change the CSV import to "keep, don't do anything", but the translation files are already created. I have to remove them. Then I drag'n'drop another CSV... and yet again, "keep", remove the dozen of "translation" files emitted... and that for every file. So I decided "screw CSVs, I'll just use JSON instead"... and then I stumbled upon this bug instead, actually breaking the import code for me (I had a schema with ints, and the code broke on deserializing the floats Godot created via conversion)... oh well, I should probably just go with XML instead xD

on a more serious note: tl;dr editor _shouldn't_ do such things without being explicitly asked to. It _shouldn't_ assume the CSV should be automatically treated as translations CSV without me telling it so. It _shouldn't_ assume it can reformat any text file I added without asking me so. This is basic UI/UX design. It should be exclusively opt-in, not opt-out, if at all. That said, the "reformatting" of JSONs should _never_ change the values themselves; it's unacceptable to have a text formatter to convert numbers without decimal dot (commonly known as "integers") to numbers with decimal dot (commonly known as "floats"). I haven't heard of ktlint or spotless doing so, and I guess if it did people would immediately report it as a bug and would stop using it, because, simply, their code would break left and right.

And, going back to "but JSON spec allows this reformatting" opinion - actually, https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/105160#issuecomment-3194609382 is 100% right. This is JSON spec:

```
number:
* integer fraction exponent

integer:
* digit
* onenine digits
* '-' digit
* '-' onenine digits
```

>A number is a sequence of decimal digits with no superfluous leading zero. It may have a preceding minus
sign (U+002D). It may have a fractional part prefixed by a decimal point (U+002E). It may have an exponent,
prefixed by e (U+0065) or E (U+0045) and optionally + (U+002B) or – (U+002D). The digits are the code
points U+0030 through U+0039.

It _may_ have a fractional part. It means it also *might not have it*. This means that `1.0` is not automatically `1` and it's also not `1E0` nor `+1.0` nor `1.00` as per the standard, because the standard is for data transfer format only and is thus not concerned with consumer semantics. Nothing in the standard says the dot is in any way mandated or required. It's not even possible to create that connection by saying "but JS doesn't have ints!", because... (quote from the spec)
>A number is very much like a C or Java number

Yes. Explicitly. Neither C nor Java conflates int literals with float literals. `1` is always considered an interger-type literal in those langs, and `1.0` a floating-point-type literal (well, technically it's a double, but the point still stands).
Each of those numeric values is distinct and it's up to consumer (parser) how those values are interpreted - whether those should be deserialized to the very same final value or not. A `number` in JSON is basically a text string with additional requirements/provisions (i.e. has to consist of 0-9 digits only with exceptions of: can have a preceding minus, can't have a preceding 0, might have a `e` or `E` exponent with optional `+` and `-`), that's all. By convention, most deserializing engines treat no-decimal-dot numbers as int-compatible on deserialization, and decimal-dot numbers as float-compatible.

As to "which of the options is the best" - I'd say _any, as long as it's merged in 2026_. It's been broken for 4 years already. I'd be fine with Option 4. JSON is a borderline case, it can be both just text and an actual resource, depending on context I'd say. Regardless, it should only be updated on-demand, if at all.

In my case the issue is:

I'm creating data in a completely separate app, I export it via JSON, then import it into my Godot project. Because both that app and my Godot project use C#, I have them use the same .cs file with all the DTO definitions.

If any of those DTO classes contain int variables (like IDs) and Godot turns them into floats, Newtonsoft (unsurprisingly) fails to deserialize them and throws an exception. Sure JSON might not differentiate between "int" and "float", but the apps that use it do, and data exchange is one of the primary uses of JSONs.

Option 4 and option 3 sound fine to me, when I first realized this was happening the Import settings was the first place I looked. I don't care about extra .imports as long as Godot isn't overwriting my files without my knowledge.

> Workaround: If you're not planning to edit the files _in the Godot editor_, then a "simple" workaround is to never `preload` the JSON file. If you manage it with just `load`s, Godot won't see fit to cannibalize your files.

I'm not using preload anywhere (I can't, since it isn't even a thing in C# scripts), I only use `FileAccess.Open()` & `FileAccess.GetAsText()` and it still happens :-(

I found [this post](https://www.reddit.com/r/godot/comments/1q441i1/godot_451_automatically_formats_json_files_after/) where OP solved it by using a custom extension, I might have to do the same since right now this feature(?) is completely breaking my project.

EDIT: Tried the .gdignore workaround, but it seems to break `FileAccess` on export, even when adding the folder to "Filters to export non-resource files/folders"

Alternatively, users could be allowed to modify the JSON file (`.json`) only in the text editor.  In the inspector, json can only be viewed, not edited.

The generic extension `.tres`  can be used for editing JSON in the inspector. Alternatively, add an **edit** button to jump to the text editor.
Just as a side note, I don't use `preload` either, but I use a direct `@export var` reference to the JSON files that get involuntarily reformatted.

@jedomed frankly? That's basically what I did at first, and it's a reasonable workaround here. Later, I just decided to go with a YAML parser, and note that JSONs are parsable as YAMLs 99% of the time (because JSONs are actually almost a subset of YAML), while being able to extend to YAML is also providing a lot of fun stuff to use that's neat for game data.
